value: avoided the den holding a strong magnet: 33 of 49 lobsters occupied the control den and 16 the magnet den
eye: whole animal (magnetic sense, receptor not identified)
method: two-choice den test in a tank: one den held a neodymium magnet, the other a non-magnetic control weight
conditions: wild Caribbean spiny lobsters caught in Florida Bay within 350 m of the Keys Marine Laboratory and tested there in July and August 2014; circular fiberglass tank 164 cm across, 23 cm of seawater, two dens at the ends of an east-west channel; 15 min trials; 51 tested, 49 analysed (those in a den at the end); ambient geomagnetic intensity 43.7 uT; magnet grade N50, surface field 703.1 mT

source.title: Size-dependent avoidance of a strong magnetic anomaly in Caribbean spiny lobsters

quote: Of the 49 lobsters that occupied a den by the end of the 15-min trial period, 33 (67%) occupied the control den and 16 (33%) occupied the magnet den (Fig. 3).
note: The authors test the choice with an exact binomial test (P=0.021) and say the reason for avoidance is not known (the field may resemble a place far from home, or may simply be unfamiliar). The experiment does not reveal which element of the magnetic field the lobsters detect. Den choice depended on size: lobsters choosing the magnet den were significantly smaller (Mann-Whitney U = 142.5, P = 0.0095) and carapace length predicted den choice (logistic regression, P = 0.019); smaller lobsters appeared indifferent and larger ones avoided the magnet den. The authors say additional studies are needed to confirm or refute that lobsters undergo a size-dependent shift in their response to magnetic fields. The anomaly was stronger than natural geological ones, so the authors urge caution in extrapolating to natural behavior. Authors and title are from the PDF itself; Crossref returned an error for this DOI.

value: females attracted to a warmed stimulus 2.5 C above ambient
eye: whole animal (heat sensing; thermoreceptor location not stated in the records)
method: landing of mosquitoes on a warmed Peltier element in a cage supplemented with CO2
conditions: wild-type females 10 to 21 days old, fasted 15 to 24 h with water; 45 to 50 mosquitoes per trial; standard ambient 26 C; 70 to 80% relative humidity; a 20 s CO2 pulse began each stimulus period; no host odor in the heat-seeking assays

source.title: The cation channel TRPA1 tunes mosquito thermotaxis to host temperatures

quote: We found that mosquitoes were highly sensitive to thermal contrast and were attracted to stimuli 2.5˚C above ambient (Figure 1D–F).
note: The stimulus is a Peltier element covered with paper, not a host, and the authors note that tissue temperature depends on contact and material properties, so it cannot reproduce a host's thermal profile. Attraction here was measured with CO2 present. The Discussion repeats that the animals can detect a thermal contrast as small as 2.5 C. Read on the eLife v1 PDF (CC BY).

value: thermotaxis driven by relative warmth and limited by an absolute upper threshold of about 50 to 55 C
eye: whole animal (heat sensing; TRPA1 tested as the candidate channel)
method: landing of mosquitoes on a Peltier element held at stimulus temperatures from ambient to 55 C or more
conditions: wild-type females 10 to 21 days old, fasted 15 to 24 h; 45 to 50 per trial; ambient 26 C (some runs at 21 and 31 C); a 20 s CO2 pulse began each stimulus period

source.title: The cation channel TRPA1 tunes mosquito thermotaxis to host temperatures

quote: These results show that Ae. aegypti thermotaxis is driven by seeking relative warmth, but restricted by an absolute upper threshold of ~50–55˚C.
note: Occupancy of the element rose with temperature up to 40 C; a 50 C stimulus drew about half as many animals as a 40 C one, and stimuli of 55 C or greater gave occupancy indistinguishable from an ambient stimulus. The abstract reports that TRPA1 mutants fail to avoid temperatures above host levels. Same Peltier-not-host caveat as the 2.5 C record.

value: avoidance response away from the IR source
method: behavioural: restrained flying beetles stimulated laterally with IR radiation from an emitter
conditions: wild adults collected January 2017 on burnt areas around Perth, Western Australia; tethered flight; emitter brought to 70 mm from the lateral abdomen; stimulus at least 7 s; intensity 48.7 mW/cm2, about 20% above the earlier electrophysiological threshold of 40 mW/cm2; 14 beetles

source.authors: Hinz M, Klein A, Schmitz A, Schmitz H
source.title: The impact of infrared radiation in flight control in the Australian firebeetle Merimna atrata

quote: After exposure, beetles always showed an avoidance response away from the IR source.
note: All 14 beetles responded with evasive maneuvers, though the threshold criterion was not reached for one beetle irradiated from the left. Reversible covering of the abdominal IR organs stopped the response (3 beetles) and it returned when the cover was removed. Beetles were never attracted to the IR source. The authors say the true threshold remains unresolved, tethered flight may have affected behavior, and beetle ages and sexes were not recorded. CC BY.

value: avoidance reactions in some beetles at 11.4 mW/cm2
method: behavioural: restrained flying beetles stimulated laterally with a weaker IR stimulus
conditions: same set-up as the 48.7 mW/cm2 test (tethered flight, emitter 70 mm from the lateral abdomen, stimulus at least 7 s); 9 beetles tested, 4 showed evasive behavior

source.authors: Hinz M, Klein A, Schmitz A, Schmitz H
source.title: The impact of infrared radiation in flight control in the Australian firebeetle Merimna atrata

quote: Tests with weaker IR radiation (11.4 mW/cm2) also induced avoidance reactions in some beetles pointing to a lower threshold.
note: Five of nine beetles did not react. The authors call the weak-stimulus results inconsistent and could not confirm a lower threshold. The IR threshold of the organs is therefore not settled by this record.

value: highest sensitivity at 300 Hz, mean threshold 116.8 +/- 3.3 dB re 1 uPa (U-shaped audiogram, 100 to 600 Hz tested)
method: auditory evoked potentials (AEP) to tone pips at 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 and 600 Hz
conditions: 114 juvenile fish (mean about 14.2 cm standard length, 70 to 80 g) from a captive aquaculture population; lightly anesthetized with MS-222 and restrained within about 1 cm of the hydrophone in a PVC container in an anechoic chamber, about 23 C; background SPL in the container 91 to 110 dB re 1 uPa; particle motion not measured

source.authors: Rojas L, Ruser A, Baltzer J, Crouzet C, Schlachter M, Schnitzler J, Siebert U, Morell M
source.title: Hearing thresholds in European sea bass (Dicentrarchus labrax): new insights into auditory sensitivity

quote: Our results revealed a U-shaped audiogram with highest sensitivity at 300 Hz (mean threshold: 116.8 ± 3.3 dB re 1 µPa), and thresholds up to 22 dB lower than previously reported.
note: Frequencies above 600 Hz were not tested, so 300 Hz is the best point within 100 to 600 Hz and gives no upper hearing limit. In a small tank pressure and particle motion cannot be fully separated; the authors say the thresholds should be read as sensitivity to particle motion. They also say AEP may underestimate true auditory sensitivity and that confined tanks add reverberation and standing waves. The lower thresholds against an earlier AEP study of 6 fish are attributed to sample size, signal processing and calibration, noise control and detection criterion. CC BY.

value: unimodal bearings along the former migration direction (d-axis) under the geomagnetic field
eye: whole animal (magnetic compass or other cue, not separated)
method: displaced toads released in a circular arena; bearings read at the outer wall (60.5 cm from the start) in the natural field
conditions: 62 male toads collected at a drift fence during the spawning migration and tested after sunset 28 March to 2 April 2010 at a car park in Vienna, Austria; 29 analysed per set-up; clustering significant only at the outer circle, with no significant pattern at the start or the 39 cm inner circle; the drift fence runs at a mean direction of 32.5 degrees

source.title: Magnetic orientation of the Common Toad: establishing an arena approach for adult anurans

quote: After displacement, toads oriented themselves unimodally under the geomagnetic field, following their former migration direction (d-axis).
note: Only males were used. The authors tentatively read the d-axis as the former migration direction and say a learned route to the tunnel, or an internal map built over years at the fence, is possible. The design did not separate magnetic from celestial cues. They suggest a longer rest after displacement and a larger arena for future work. CC BY.

value: bimodal bearings along the d-axis when the magnetic field was reversed
eye: whole animal (magnetic compass or other cue, not separated)
method: displaced toads released in a circular arena with the horizontal magnetic field reversed; bearings read at the outer wall
conditions: male toads from the same collection and arena as the natural-field run, each toad tested once (62 tested, 29 analysed per set-up); only the horizontal field component reversed with Helmholtz coils; outer circle 60.5 cm; no significant pattern at the start or the inner circle

source.title: Magnetic orientation of the Common Toad: establishing an arena approach for adult anurans

quote: When the magnetic field was reversed, the distribution of bearings changed from a unimodal to a bimodal pattern, but still along the d-axis.
note: The unimodal test at the wall was not significant under the reversed field (mean 305 degrees, r = 0.28, Rayleigh P = 0.10, n = 29). The authors suggest a cue conflict, with some toads following magnetic and others celestial cues; the design did not separate these.
